fp2_differentiation_implicit.description: Find first and second derivatives on a regular implicit branch and use them to determine the tangent and concavity.

sections.title: Why does differentiating y² introduce y′?
sections.label: Differentiate the whole relation
sections.intro: On a smooth branch, \(y\) varies with \(x\) even if the relation does not give an explicit formula for \(y\). The chain rule is applied wherever \(y\) appears.

blocks.html: \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(y^2)=2yy'\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}(xy)=y+xy'\). Differentiate each term once, then collect all terms containing \(y'\).
Treating \(y\) as constant while differentiating with respect to \(x\) loses its contribution to the slope.
Write the derivative equation before substituting the point.

blocks.title: Collect terms in the gradient
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(1,-1\right)\) on \(X Y + X + 3 Y^{2} + 2 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 1\) and \(Y=y + 1\), find the gradient of the tangent.
blocks.hint: Remember that the derivative of Y with respect to x is y′.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(Y + 1+\left(X + 6 Y + 2\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(1+2y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=- \frac{1}{2}\).

blocks.title: Differentiate a product of centred coordinates
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(3,2\right)\) on \(2 X^{2} + 3 X Y + 2 X - Y^{2} + 5 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 3\) and \(Y=y - 2\), find the gradient of the tangent.
blocks.hint: Remember that the derivative of Y with respect to x is y′.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(4 X + 3 Y + 2+\left(3 X - 2 Y + 5\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(2+5y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=- \frac{2}{5}\).

sections.title: When can I divide to find the slope?
sections.label: Check the regular branch
sections.intro: After collecting \(y'\) the equation has form \(F_x+F_y y'=0\). Here \(F_x\) and \(F_y\) are derivatives of the defining expression holding the other coordinate fixed.

blocks.html: If \(F_y\ne0\) at the point then the tangent has finite gradient \(-\frac{F_x}{F_y}\). When \(F_y=0\) but \(F_x\ne0\), use \(x\) locally as a function of \(y\) to recognise a vertical tangent.

figure.alt: At the rightmost point the circle has a vertical tangent. At the top its tangent is horizontal.
figure.caption: At the rightmost point the circle has a vertical tangent. At the top its tangent is horizontal.

blocks.html: If both derivatives vanish, this method alone gives no definite tangent. Do not infer a horizontal line from the identity \(0=0\).
Check the point lies on the curve and substitute in the denominator separately.

blocks.title: Read a positive gradient
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(2,-2\right)\) on \(X^{2} - 3 X + 2 Y^{2} + 2 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 2\) and \(Y=y + 2\), find the gradient of the tangent.
blocks.hint: Remember that the derivative of Y with respect to x is y′.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(2 X - 3+\left(4 Y + 2\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(-3+2y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=\frac{3}{2}\).

sections.title: Which new terms appear on a second differentiation?
sections.label: Apply the product rule again
sections.intro: The first derivative equation involves a product between a possibly variable coefficient and \(y'\). Differentiate both factors before evaluating at the point.

blocks.html: For a twice differentiable polynomial relation, \(F_{xx}+2F_{xy}y'+F_{yy}(y')^2+F_y y''=0\). For example, a term \(F_y y'\) contributes \(F_y y''\) and \((F_{yx}+F_{yy}y')y'\).
A computed value of \(y'\) holds at one point. Replacing \(y'\) by that constant before differentiating erases \(y''\).
Keep all of \(x\), \(y\) and \(y'\) until the second derivative relation is complete.

blocks.title: Find both derivative orders
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(1,3\right)\) on \(X^{2} - 2 X Y + 2 X + 3 Y^{2} - 3 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 1\) and \(Y=y - 3\), find both first and second derivatives of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).
blocks.hint: Differentiate the relationship twice while treating Y as a function of x.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(2 X - 2 Y + 2+\left(- 2 X + 6 Y - 3\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(2-3y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=\frac{2}{3}\).

Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).

At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=\frac{2}{3}\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(-3\) and is nonzero.

blocks.title: Keep the squared first derivative term
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(-1,1\right)\) on \(2 X^{2} + X Y + X - Y^{2} + 3 Y=0\), where \(X=x + 1\) and \(Y=y - 1\), find both first and second derivatives of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).
blocks.hint: Differentiate the relationship twice while treating Y as a function of x.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(4 X + Y + 1+\left(X - 2 Y + 3\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(1+3y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=- \frac{1}{3}\).

Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).

At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=- \frac{28}{27}\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(3\) and is nonzero.

sections.title: How do I use the slope in a tangent or normal?
sections.label: Choose the correct line
sections.intro: A slope describes a line only when combined with its point. The tangent and normal share that point and are perpendicular.

blocks.html: For a finite nonzero tangent slope \(m\), the normal has slope \(-\frac1m\). If one line is horizontal, the other is vertical.
Negating the gradient alone generally does not make the line perpendicular. Take the negative reciprocal.
A line written \(y-y_0=m(x-x_0)\) displays its point and slope for a quick substitution check.

blocks.title: Reverse the normal slope
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(1,4\right)\) on \(- X^{2} + X Y - 4 X + 2 Y^{2} + 3 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 1\) and \(Y=y - 4\), find the gradients of the tangent and normal.
blocks.hint: Solve the first derivative equation. Then use perpendicularity.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(- 2 X + Y - 4+\left(X + 4 Y + 3\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(-4+3y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=\frac{4}{3}\).

Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).

At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=- \frac{70}{27}\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(3\) and is nonzero.

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so use the negative reciprocal \(- \frac{3}{4}\).

sections.title: What does the sign of the second derivative show?
sections.label: Interpret local concavity
sections.intro: The second derivative measures how the gradient of a regular branch changes with \(x\). A point need not be stationary for this to be useful.

blocks.html: If \(y''>0\) the branch is locally concave up, and if \(y''<0\) it is locally concave down. Only with \(y'=0\) does this nonzero value classify a local extremum.
Positive curvature of the graph in the sense of \(y''>0\) does not say the current gradient is positive.
Give the numerical slope and concavity separately when both are requested.

blocks.title: Read the concavity without assuming stationarity
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(2,1\right)\) on \(2 X^{2} + 2 X + 2 Y^{2} + 3 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 2\) and \(Y=y - 1\), find the second derivative and state the local concavity.
blocks.hint: Differentiate before substituting any numerical value for the slope.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(4 X + 2+\left(4 Y + 3\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(2+3y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=- \frac{2}{3}\).

Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).

At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=- \frac{52}{27}\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(3\) and is nonzero.

Its sign gives concave down on this smooth branch.

revision.body: Differentiate all terms with the chain rule. Solve \(F_x+F_y y'=0\). Differentiate that relation again before substituting a point or a numerical slope.
revision.checks:
• Where does the second copy of \(F_{xy}y'\) come from?
  • What happens when \(F_y=0\) but \(F_x\ne0\)?
  • Can \(y''>0\) occur when \(y'<0\)?

fp2_differentiation_parametric.description: Calculate exact parametric first and second derivatives and classify horizontal or vertical tangents.

sections.title: Why does a parametric slope use a quotient?
sections.label: Share the same parameter
sections.intro: Both coordinates depend on \(t\). When \(x\) can serve as a local input, the chain rule gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\).

blocks.html: If \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\ne0\), divide to get \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}\). The numerator and denominator belong to the same parameter value.
Dividing the coordinate functions \(y(t)\) and \(x(t)\) is different from dividing their derivatives.
Write both derivatives next to the original coordinate equations.

blocks.title: Evaluate on a different point
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 3 t + 1\) and \(y=2 t^{2} + 4 t + 1\). At \(t=1\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
blocks.hint: The derivative of the gradient with respect to t needs one further division.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 4\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t + 4}{2 t + 3}\) and hence \(\frac{8}{5}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{4}{\left(2 t + 3\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{4}{125}\).

blocks.title: Use a half as the parameter
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(x=2 t^{2} + 2 t\) and \(y=- t^{2} + t + 3\). At \(t=\frac{1}{2}\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
blocks.hint: The derivative of the gradient with respect to t needs one further division.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=1 - 2 t\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{1 - 2 t}{4 t + 2}\) and hence \(0\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{1}{\left(- 2 t - 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(- \frac{1}{8}\).

sections.title: Why is there a second division when finding y″?
sections.label: Differentiate the gradient
sections.intro: The slope is now a function of \(t\). Its derivative with respect to \(t\) is a rate of change along the parameter. Convert it to a rate per unit \(x\).

blocks.html: \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac1{x'(t)}\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\!\left(\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}\right)=\frac{y''(t)x'(t)-y'(t)x''(t)}{(x'(t))^3}\).
\(\frac{y''(t)}{x''(t)}\) is not the second derivative of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).
Write the outer factor \(\frac1{x'(t)}\) before differentiating inside the brackets.

blocks.title: The second derivative uses another division
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 2 t + 3\) and \(y=2 t^{2} + t\). At \(t=1\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
blocks.hint: The derivative of the gradient with respect to t needs one further division.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 1\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t + 1}{2 t + 2}\) and hence \(\frac{5}{4}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{3}{4 \left(t + 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{3}{32}\).

sections.title: How does the direction of the parameter affect signs?
sections.label: Respect signed motion
sections.intro: A parameter may traverse an arc from right to left. The denominator of the slope, \(x'(t)\), is a signed derivative.

blocks.html: The chain-rule quotient automatically gives the slope with respect to increasing \(x\). Keep the signed \(x'(t)\) again in the second derivative formula.
Using \(|x'(t)|\) changes the slope whenever the parameter moves left.
Report the coordinate pair by evaluating \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) at the same \(t\).

blocks.title: Keep the sign when x is decreasing
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(x=- t^{2} - 2 t - 1\) and \(y=2 t^{2} + t + 1\). At \(t=2\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
blocks.hint: The derivative of the gradient with respect to t needs one further division.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=- 2 t - 2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 1\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t + 1}{- 2 t - 2}\) and hence \(- \frac{3}{2}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{3}{4 \left(t + 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{1}{36}\).

blocks.title: Apply the quotient rule exactly
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(x=t^{2} - 3 t + 3\) and \(y=2 t^{2} - 2 t + 1\). At \(t=0\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
blocks.hint: The derivative of the gradient with respect to t needs one further division.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t - 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t - 2\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t - 2}{2 t - 3}\) and hence \(\frac{2}{3}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{8}{\left(3 - 2 t\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{8}{27}\).

sections.title: When can the tangent or normal be vertical?
sections.label: Tangent orientation
sections.intro: If \(y'(t)=0\) and \(x'(t)\ne0\), the tangent is horizontal. If \(x'(t)=0\) and \(y'(t)\ne0\), the tangent is vertical on the regular parametric curve.

blocks.html: For a finite nonzero tangent slope \(m\), the normal slope is \(-\frac1m\). For a zero tangent slope, give the vertical normal equation instead of dividing by zero.
When both parameter derivatives vanish, neither quotient can be used directly. Examine the local curve or limiting slopes.
Check regularity before dividing or taking a reciprocal.

blocks.title: Choose the perpendicular gradient
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(x=- t^{2} - t\) and \(y=3 t^{2} + 4 t - 1\). At \(t=1\), give the gradient of the normal.
blocks.hint: Find the tangent first using a quotient of parameter derivatives.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=- 2 t - 1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=6 t + 4\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{6 t + 4}{- 2 t - 1}\) and hence \(- \frac{10}{3}\) at the specified parameter.

Take the negative reciprocal to obtain \(\frac{3}{10}\).

sections.title: How do I classify a regular horizontal tangent?
sections.label: Use the correct second derivative
sections.intro: Find candidate parameter values from \(y'(t)=0\). Retain only those with \(x'(t)\ne0\) when using this derivative test.

blocks.html: At a regular stationary point, \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{y''(t)}{(x'(t))^2}\). Thus its sign there agrees with \(y''(t)\). If it is zero, compare the slope around the point.
The simpler formula holds at a horizontal stationary point, not at an arbitrary parameter.
Use the full derivative formula first when the tangent fails to be horizontal.

blocks.title: Horizontal tangent with a local maximum
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(x=- t^{2} - 2 t + 2\) and \(y=1 - 3 t^{2}\). At \(t=0\), classify the point and give its second derivative.
blocks.hint: Verify a regular horizontal tangent before using the second-derivative test.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=- 2 t - 2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=- 6 t\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- \frac{6 t}{- 2 t - 2}\) and hence \(0\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{3}{2 \left(- t - 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(- \frac{3}{2}\).

The slope vanishes and the second derivative is negative. Hence the point is a local maximum.

examples.title: Differentiate two coordinate functions
examples.question: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 2 t + 1\) and \(y=2 t^{2} + 3 t - 1\). At \(t=1\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
solution: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 3\).
Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t + 3}{2 t + 2}\) and hence \(\frac{7}{4}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{1}{4 \left(t + 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{1}{32}\).

examples.title: Work at a fractional parameter
examples.question: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 3 t + 2\) and \(y=3 t^{2} + 2 t\). At \(t=\frac{1}{2}\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
solution: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=6 t + 2\).
Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{6 t + 2}{2 t + 3}\) and hence \(\frac{5}{4}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{14}{\left(2 t + 3\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{7}{32}\).

examples.title: Find the missing factor of the first coordinate derivative
examples.question: A curve has \(x=2 t^{2} + t + 1\) and \(y=- 2 t^{2} + 5 t + 3\). At \(t=2\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
solution: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=5 - 4 t\).
Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{5 - 4 t}{4 t + 1}\) and hence \(- \frac{1}{3}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{24}{\left(- 4 t - 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(- \frac{8}{243}\).

examples.title: The parameter moves from right to left
examples.question: A curve has \(x=- t^{2} - 3 t + 3\) and \(y=t^{2} + 2 t + 4\). At \(t=1\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
solution: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=- 2 t - 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 2\).
Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{2 t + 2}{- 2 t - 3}\) and hence \(- \frac{4}{5}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{2}{\left(2 t + 3\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{2}{125}\).

examples.title: Keep the cubic denominator
examples.question: A curve has \(x=t^{2} - t\) and \(y=- 2 t^{2} + t + 1\). At \(t=0\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
solution: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t - 1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=1 - 4 t\).
Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{1 - 4 t}{2 t - 1}\) and hence \(-1\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{2}{\left(2 t - 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(-2\).

examples.title: Get the gradient of the normal
examples.question: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 3 t + 5\) and \(y=2 t^{2} - 2 t + 1\). At \(t=0\), give the gradient of the normal.
solution: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t - 2\).
Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t - 2}{2 t + 3}\) and hence \(- \frac{2}{3}\) at the specified parameter.
Take the negative reciprocal to obtain \(\frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Classify a regular horizontal tangent
examples.question: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 2 t + 1\) and \(y=3 t^{2} - 1\). At \(t=0\), classify the point and give its second derivative.
solution: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=6 t\).
Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{6 t}{2 t + 2}\) and hence \(0\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{3}{2 \left(t + 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{3}{2}\).
The slope vanishes and the second derivative is positive. Hence the point is a local minimum.

extraPractice.title: Evaluate a nonstationary gradient and concavity
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has \(x=2 t^{2} + 3 t + 2\) and \(y=t^{2} + 3 t + 1\). At \(t=1\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
extraPractice.hint: The derivative of the gradient with respect to t needs one further division.
extraPractice.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 3\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{2 t + 3}{4 t + 3}\) and hence \(\frac{5}{7}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{6}{\left(- 4 t - 3\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(- \frac{6}{343}\).

extraPractice.title: A finite slope at a negative parameter
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has \(x=- t^{2} + 2 t + 1\) and \(y=3 t^{2} + 2 t + 1\). At \(t=-1\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
extraPractice.hint: The derivative of the gradient with respect to t needs one further division.
extraPractice.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 - 2 t\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=6 t + 2\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{6 t + 2}{2 - 2 t}\) and hence \(-1\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{2}{\left(1 - t\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

extraPractice.title: Check the sign of a normal slope
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 3 t\) and \(y=2 t^{2} - t\). At \(t=1\), give the gradient of the normal.
extraPractice.hint: Find the tangent first using a quotient of parameter derivatives.
extraPractice.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t - 1\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t - 1}{2 t + 3}\) and hence \(\frac{3}{5}\) at the specified parameter.

Take the negative reciprocal to obtain \(- \frac{5}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: Classification at an off-zero parameter
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 3 t + 4\) and \(y=- 2 t^{2} + 4 t + 1\). At \(t=1\), classify the point and give its second derivative.
extraPractice.hint: Verify a regular horizontal tangent before using the second-derivative test.
extraPractice.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 - 4 t\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 - 4 t}{2 t + 3}\) and hence \(0\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{20}{\left(- 2 t - 3\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(- \frac{4}{25}\).

The slope vanishes and the second derivative is negative. Hence the point is a local maximum.

extraPractice.title: Classification with negative parameter speed
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has \(x=- t^{2} - t + 2\) and \(y=t^{2} + 2 t + 1\). At \(t=-1\), classify the point and give its second derivative.
extraPractice.hint: Verify a regular horizontal tangent before using the second-derivative test.
extraPractice.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=- 2 t - 1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 2\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{2 t + 2}{- 2 t - 1}\) and hence \(0\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{2}{\left(- 2 t - 1\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(2\).

The slope vanishes and the second derivative is positive. Hence the point is a local minimum.

glossary.definition: An input \(t\) controlling both coordinates.
A point where at least one coordinate derivative is nonzero.
The rate of change of the gradient with respect to \(x\).
A point of a locally differentiable graph where the gradient is zero.

revision.body: Write \(m=\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}\), then \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac1{x'(t)}\frac{\mathrm dm}{\mathrm dt}\) where \(x'(t)\ne0\). Keep signs, and substitute the parameter at the end.
revision.checks:
• Why is \(x'(t)\) used twice?
  • Which conditions give a vertical tangent?
  • When is the formula \(\frac{y''(t)}{(x'(t))^2}\) valid?
revision.examTip: Show both divisions in your working. Keep the parameter of a candidate separate from its coordinates.

fp2_differentiation_functions.description: Derive the hyperbolic and inverse-function derivative rules and apply them with the correct branch and chain factors.

sections.title: Why do sinh and cosh differentiate into each other?
sections.label: Differentiate the definitions
sections.intro: Their definitions use exponentials with opposite exponents. Differentiating \(\mathrm e^{-x}\) contributes an extra minus sign.

blocks.html: \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\sinh x=\cosh x\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\cosh x=\sinh x\). For a quotient, \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\tanh x=\operatorname{sech}^2x\) follows from \(\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1\).
Borrowing the minus sign from the derivative of ordinary cosine gives the wrong derivative for hyperbolic cosine.
Check the derivative of \(\sinh x\) at zero: the value should be one.

blocks.title: Find a sine derivative at the centre
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\sinh{\left(4 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{1}{4})\) and \(f''(\frac{1}{4})\).
blocks.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
blocks.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=4 x - 1\), with derivative \(4\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\cosh{\left(u \right)}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=4 \cosh{\left(4 x - 1 \right)}\). Substitute \(u=0\) to get \(4\).

Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(16 \sinh{\left(4 x - 1 \right)}\) and so the stated value is \(0\).

blocks.title: Check the maximum slope of the quotient
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\tanh{\left(5 x + 2 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(- \frac{2}{5})\).
blocks.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
blocks.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=5 x + 2\), with derivative \(5\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(1 - \tanh^{2}{\left(u \right)}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=5 - 5 \tanh^{2}{\left(5 x + 2 \right)}\). Substitute \(u=0\) to get \(5\).

sections.title: How can I differentiate the inverse of a function?
sections.label: Reverse the derivative
sections.intro: Write \(y=f^{-1}(x)\) as \(x=f(y)\) on the correct original branch. Differentiate this equation before reversing the derivative.

blocks.html: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac1{f'(y)}\) where \(f'(y)\ne0\). Use a branch restriction to choose a square-root sign and write the result in terms of \(x\).
The derivative of an inverse function is not the reciprocal of the derivative evaluated at the same input; evaluate at the inverse output.
State the domain where the derivative is finite.

blocks.title: Use the inverse output branch
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(x)=- \sinh^{-1}{\left(3 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{7}{36})\).
blocks.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
blocks.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=1 - 3 x\), with derivative \(-3\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{u^{2} + 1}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=- \frac{3}{\sqrt{\left(1 - 3 x\right)^{2} + 1}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{5}{12}\) to get \(- \frac{36}{13}\).

sections.title: Why do inverse sine and cosine have opposite signs?
sections.label: Use the principal circular branches
sections.intro: On the inverse sine branch \(-\frac\pi2\le y\le\frac\pi2\), cosine is nonnegative. On the inverse cosine branch \(0\le y\le\pi\), sine is nonnegative.

blocks.html: \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\sin^{-1}x=\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\cos^{-1}x=-\frac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\) for \(|x|<1\).
Differentiating cosine contributes a minus before the derivative is inverted.
The inverse functions have endpoint values, but their finite derivatives here apply only on the open interval.

blocks.title: Recover a signed inverse sine slope
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(x)=- \sin^{-1}{\left(2 x - 2 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{3}{5})\).
blocks.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
blocks.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=2 - 2 x\), with derivative \(-2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=- \frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - \left(2 - 2 x\right)^{2}}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{4}{5}\) to get \(- \frac{10}{3}\).

blocks.title: Keep a negative outer derivative
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\cos^{-1}{\left(4 x - 3 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{9}{10})\).
blocks.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
blocks.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=4 x - 3\), with derivative \(4\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(- \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=- \frac{4}{\sqrt{1 - \left(4 x - 3\right)^{2}}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{3}{5}\) to get \(-5\).

sections.title: How do the inverse hyperbolic domains affect their derivatives?
sections.label: Use the hyperbolic inverse rules
sections.intro: The square-root sign and denominator depend on which direct function is being inverted.

blocks.html: The derivatives of \(\sinh^{-1}x\), \(\cosh^{-1}x\) and \(\tanh^{-1}x\) are respectively \(\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\), \(\frac1{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\) and \(\frac1{1-x^2}\). Their real derivative domains are all real \(x\), \(x>1\), and \(|x|<1\).
The derivative of inverse hyperbolic cosine is not finite at \(x=1\) though the inverse itself is defined there.
Apply domain restrictions to the whole inner expression in a composition.

blocks.title: Calculate a finite inverse cosh derivative
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\cosh^{-1}{\left(3 x \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{13}{15})\).
blocks.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
blocks.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=3 x\), with derivative \(3\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{u - 1} \sqrt{u + 1}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3 x - 1} \sqrt{3 x + 1}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{13}{5}\) to get \(\frac{5}{4}\).

sections.title: How do I apply these rules twice to a composition?
sections.label: Differentiate the full product
sections.intro: With a composite function, the first derivative has an inner-derivative factor. It may need differentiating in the second step.

blocks.html: For \(F(x)=f(u(x))\), \(F''(x)=f''(u(x))(u'(x))^2+f'(u(x))u''(x)\). The second term vanishes for a linear inner function.
The chain factor appears again after differentiation. A single power of the inner scale is insufficient for the second derivative of a linear composition.
Keep exact signs and radicals throughout.

blocks.title: Keep both inner factors
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\tanh^{-1}{\left(2 x - 3 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{4}{3})\) and \(f''(\frac{4}{3})\).
blocks.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
blocks.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=2 x - 3\), with derivative \(2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{1 - u^{2}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{2}{1 - \left(2 x - 3\right)^{2}}\). Substitute \(u=- \frac{1}{3}\) to get \(\frac{9}{4}\).

Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(\frac{8 \left(2 x - 3\right)}{\left(\left(2 x - 3\right)^{2} - 1\right)^{2}}\) and so the stated value is \(- \frac{27}{8}\).

examples.title: Differentiate a hyperbolic sine at argument zero
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\sinh{\left(3 x - 2 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{2}{3})\) and \(f''(\frac{2}{3})\).
solution: Use the inner function \(u=3 x - 2\), with derivative \(3\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\cosh{\left(u \right)}\).
The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=3 \cosh{\left(3 x - 2 \right)}\). Substitute \(u=0\) to get \(3\).
Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(9 \sinh{\left(3 x - 2 \right)}\) and so the stated value is \(0\).

examples.title: Find the derivative sign of a shifted cosh
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\cosh{\left(2 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{1}{2})\) and \(f''(\frac{1}{2})\).
solution: Use the inner function \(u=1 - 2 x\), with derivative \(-2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\sinh{\left(u \right)}\).
The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=2 \sinh{\left(2 x - 1 \right)}\). Substitute \(u=0\) to get \(0\).
Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(4 \cosh{\left(2 x - 1 \right)}\) and so the stated value is \(4\).

examples.title: Derive a reciprocal square root
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\sinh^{-1}{\left(2 x + 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(- \frac{1}{8})\).
solution: Use the inner function \(u=2 x + 1\), with derivative \(2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{u^{2} + 1}}\).
The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\left(2 x + 1\right)^{2} + 1}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{3}{4}\) to get \(\frac{8}{5}\).

examples.title: Differentiate inverse sine
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}{\left(2 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{4}{5})\).
solution: Use the inner function \(u=2 x - 1\), with derivative \(2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\).
The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - \left(2 x - 1\right)^{2}}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{3}{5}\) to get \(\frac{5}{2}\).

examples.title: Keep the inverse cosine sign
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\cos^{-1}{\left(3 x + 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(- \frac{6}{13})\).
solution: Use the inner function \(u=3 x + 1\), with derivative \(3\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(- \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\).
The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=- \frac{3}{\sqrt{1 - \left(3 x + 1\right)^{2}}}\). Substitute \(u=- \frac{5}{13}\) to get \(- \frac{13}{4}\).

examples.title: Stay above the inverse cosh branch endpoint
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\cosh^{-1}{\left(2 x + 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{1}{3})\).
solution: Use the inner function \(u=2 x + 1\), with derivative \(2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{u - 1} \sqrt{u + 1}}\).
The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{x} \sqrt{2 x + 2}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{5}{3}\) to get \(\frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Differentiate the quotient rule result again
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\tanh^{-1}{\left(3 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{1}{2})\) and \(f''(\frac{1}{2})\).
solution: Use the inner function \(u=3 x - 1\), with derivative \(3\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{1 - u^{2}}\).
The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{3}{1 - \left(3 x - 1\right)^{2}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{1}{2}\) to get \(4\).
Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(\frac{18 \left(3 x - 1\right)}{\left(\left(3 x - 1\right)^{2} - 1\right)^{2}}\) and so the stated value is \(16\).

extraPractice.title: Use an exact radical if needed
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\cosh^{-1}{\left(2 x + 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(1)\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=2 x + 1\), with derivative \(2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{u - 1} \sqrt{u + 1}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{x} \sqrt{2 x + 2}}\). Substitute \(u=3\) to get \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Differentiate inverse sine twice
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}{\left(2 x + 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(- \frac{1}{5})\) and \(f''(- \frac{1}{5})\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=2 x + 1\), with derivative \(2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - \left(2 x + 1\right)^{2}}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{3}{5}\) to get \(\frac{5}{2}\).

Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(\frac{4 \left(2 x + 1\right)}{\left(1 - \left(2 x + 1\right)^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\) and so the stated value is \(\frac{75}{16}\).

extraPractice.title: A fractional inner scale
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\sinh^{-1}{\left(\frac{x}{2} + 2 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(- \frac{5}{2})\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=\frac{x}{2} + 2\), with derivative \(\frac{1}{2}\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{u^{2} + 1}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\left(\frac{x}{2} + 2\right)^{2} + 1}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{3}{4}\) to get \(\frac{2}{5}\).

extraPractice.title: Differentiate cosh twice at zero
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\cosh{\left(4 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{1}{4})\) and \(f''(\frac{1}{4})\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=4 x - 1\), with derivative \(4\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\sinh{\left(u \right)}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=4 \sinh{\left(4 x - 1 \right)}\). Substitute \(u=0\) to get \(0\).

Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(16 \cosh{\left(4 x - 1 \right)}\) and so the stated value is \(16\).

extraPractice.title: Check the sign in the inverse cosine second derivative
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\cos^{-1}{\left(2 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{1}{5})\) and \(f''(\frac{1}{5})\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=2 x - 1\), with derivative \(2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(- \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=- \frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - \left(2 x - 1\right)^{2}}}\). Substitute \(u=- \frac{3}{5}\) to get \(- \frac{5}{2}\).

Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(- \frac{4 \left(2 x - 1\right)}{\left(1 - \left(2 x - 1\right)^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\) and so the stated value is \(\frac{75}{16}\).

glossary.definition: The quantity \(u(x)\) substituted into the outside function.
The restricted original domain defining a single-valued inverse.
The reciprocal of the direct derivative evaluated at the inverse output.
An input where the relevant derivative formula is finite and defined.

revision.body: Differentiate \(\sinh\) and \(\cosh\) with a positive sign. To derive an inverse formula, differentiate \(x=f(y)\) on the principal branch, take the reciprocal, then apply the inner chain factor.
revision.checks:

  • Which inverse circular derivative is negative?

fp2_differentiation_geometry.description: Classify stationary points with the second derivative or a sign check, including flat extrema and stationary inflections.

sections.title: How do I identify a regular stationary point?
sections.label: Find a horizontal tangent
sections.intro: On a graph a stationary point has slope zero. For parametric data, use \(y'(t)=0\) together with \(x'(t)\ne0\). For implicit data, use \(F_x=0\) and \(F_y\ne0\).

blocks.html: Find the candidate first, then its coordinates. If \(y''>0\) there is a local minimum, and if \(y''<0\) there is a local maximum.
The condition \(y'(t)=0\) is insufficient when both coordinate derivatives vanish.
Verify regularity and classify at the same parameter value.

blocks.title: Classify a minimum from two coordinate derivatives
blocks.prompt: For \(x=t^{2} + 3 t + 2\) and \(y=2 t^{2} + 1\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
blocks.hint: Check both the slope and whether local monotonicity changes. The zero second derivative alone does not classify a point.
blocks.solution:
Since \(x'(0)=3\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.

The second derivative at the point is \(\frac{4}{9}\). Its sign gives the nature of this stationary point.

The one-sided gradients have opposite signs, consistent with a local minimum.

blocks.title: Read the sign at a maximum
blocks.prompt: For \(x=t^{2} + t + 3\) and \(y=2 - 2 t^{2}\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
blocks.hint: Check both the slope and whether local monotonicity changes. The zero second derivative alone does not classify a point.
blocks.solution:
Since \(x'(0)=1\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.

The second derivative at the point is \(-4\). Its sign gives the nature of this stationary point.

The one-sided gradients have opposite signs, consistent with a local maximum.

sections.title: Can y″ vanish at a point that still turns?
sections.label: Check a degenerate candidate
sections.intro: A zero second derivative rules out using that test. Look just to the left and right at the sign of the first derivative.

blocks.html: For \(y=x^4\) the gradient is negative before zero and positive after zero. The point is a minimum even though the second derivative is zero there.
Calling every point with \(y'=y''=0\) a stationary point of inflection incorrectly classifies a flat minimum or maximum.
Use a sign comparison involving the first nonzero factor of the gradient.

blocks.title: A fourth-power local maximum
blocks.prompt: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=2 - \left(x - 1\right)^{4}\) at \(x=1\).
blocks.hint: If the second derivative is zero, use the sign of the derivative on both sides.
blocks.solution:
The first derivative is \(- 4 \left(x - 1\right)^{3}\), so it vanishes at \(x=1\). The point is \(\left(1,2\right)\).

The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is positive just left and negative just right, from the parity of the factor \(\left(x - 1\right)^{3}\).

This gives a local maximum.

sections.title: When does a curve continue through a stationary point?
sections.label: Stationary point of inflection
sections.intro: A smooth branch can flatten out while staying increasing, or flatten out while staying decreasing. At a stationary inflection, its concavity changes across the point.

blocks.html: For \(y=x^3\), the gradient \(3x^2\) is positive either side of zero, whereas \(y''=6x\) changes sign. The horizontal tangent therefore occurs at a stationary point of inflection.

figure.alt: Both curves have a horizontal tangent and zero second derivative at the origin. The fourth-power curve turns there. The cubic continues increasing.
figure.caption: Both curves have a horizontal tangent and zero second derivative at the origin. The fourth-power curve turns there. The cubic continues increasing.

blocks.html: A stationary point of inflection is sometimes grouped under a textbook heading about turning points. Its gradient keeps its sign on both sides, so it is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum.
Identify the sign pattern and the change of concavity to justify this classification.

blocks.title: Look for changed concavity
blocks.prompt: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=3 \left(x - 4\right)^{3} + 2\) at \(x=4\).
blocks.hint: If the second derivative is zero, use the sign of the derivative on both sides.
blocks.solution:
The first derivative is \(9 \left(x - 4\right)^{2}\), so it vanishes at \(x=4\). The point is \(\left(4,2\right)\).

The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is positive just left and positive just right, from the parity of the factor \(\left(x - 4\right)^{2}\).

This gives a stationary point of inflection. Here the second derivative also changes sign across the point.

blocks.title: A decreasing fifth-order branch
blocks.prompt: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=1 - \left(x + 2\right)^{5}\) at \(x=-2\).
blocks.hint: If the second derivative is zero, use the sign of the derivative on both sides.
blocks.solution:
The first derivative is \(- 5 \left(x + 2\right)^{4}\), so it vanishes at \(x=-2\). The point is \(\left(-2,1\right)\).

The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is negative just left and negative just right, from the parity of the factor \(\left(x + 2\right)^{4}\).

This gives a stationary point of inflection. Here the second derivative also changes sign across the point.

sections.title: How can regular curves have non-finite gradients?
sections.label: Read the tangent direction
sections.intro: The tangent direction can be found from the nonzero parameter derivative vector. The usual slope is defined only if that vector has a nonzero horizontal component.

blocks.html: If \(x'(t)=0\) and \(y'(t)\ne0\), the tangent is vertical. If both vanish, first derivatives do not give a tangent direction by themselves.
Do not confuse a derivative that approaches infinity with one that equals zero.
When reporting a vertical tangent, write \(x=x_0\) and give the corresponding point.

blocks.title: A vertical tangent from t signs
blocks.prompt: For \(x=t^{2} + 2\) and \(y=2 t + 3\), which statement about \(t=0\) follows from the first derivatives?
blocks.hint: Look at both coordinate derivatives. One vanishing component is different from both vanishing.
blocks.solution:
At \(t=0\), the parameter derivatives are \(0\) and \(2\).

The motion has a nonzero vertical derivative and zero horizontal one. The tangent is the vertical line \(x=2\).

sections.title: How do parameter signs relate to the left and right of a point?
sections.label: Check the local orientation
sections.intro: If \(x'(t)<0\) near the point, increasing \(t\) takes you from the right of the point to the left. A signed gradient is still measured with respect to increasing \(x\).

blocks.html: Use \(x'(t)\) to identify which neighbouring parameter corresponds to the left side of the graph. Classification by a nonzero second derivative already accounts for this via the chain rule.
Using increasing parameter order as increasing \(x\) can swap a maximum and a minimum in a signed first-derivative test.
If the second derivative test gives zero, check either signs in increasing \(x\) or change of concavity explicitly.

blocks.title: Stationary point while x decreases
blocks.prompt: For \(x=- t^{2} - 3 t + 2\) and \(y=t^{3} + 1\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
blocks.hint: Check both the slope and whether local monotonicity changes. The zero second derivative alone does not classify a point.
blocks.solution:
Since \(x'(0)=-3\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.

The second derivative is zero at the point. Nearby, \(\frac{3 t^{2}}{- 2 t - 3}\) keeps the same sign on either side, because the denominator keeps the sign of \(-3\) and the numerator is a positive multiple of \(t^2\).

The curve continues the same monotonic behaviour through the horizontal tangent and changes concavity there.

examples.title: Find the minimum from a nonzero derivative
examples.question: For \(x=t^{2} + 2 t + 1\) and \(y=2 t^{2} + 2\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
solution: Since \(x'(0)=2\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.
The second derivative at the point is \(1\). Its sign gives the nature of this stationary point.
The one-sided gradients have opposite signs, consistent with a local minimum.

examples.title: Check the regular maximum
examples.question: For \(x=- t^{2} + 2 t + 3\) and \(y=1 - 2 t^{2}\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
solution: Since \(x'(0)=2\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.
The second derivative at the point is \(-1\). Its sign gives the nature of this stationary point.
The one-sided gradients have opposite signs, consistent with a local maximum.

examples.title: A flat minimum can still turn
examples.question: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=2 \left(x - 1\right)^{4} + 3\) at \(x=1\).
solution: The first derivative is \(8 \left(x - 1\right)^{3}\), so it vanishes at \(x=1\). The point is \(\left(1,3\right)\).
The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is negative just left and positive just right, from the parity of the factor \(\left(x - 1\right)^{3}\).
This gives a local minimum.

examples.title: A cubic that continues through the point
examples.question: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=\left(x - 2\right)^{3} + 4\) at \(x=2\).
solution: The first derivative is \(3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2}\), so it vanishes at \(x=2\). The point is \(\left(2,4\right)\).
The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is positive just left and positive just right, from the parity of the factor \(\left(x - 2\right)^{2}\).
This gives a stationary point of inflection. Here the second derivative also changes sign across the point.

examples.title: A decreasing stationary inflection
examples.question: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=4 - 2 \left(x + 1\right)^{5}\) at \(x=-1\).
solution: The first derivative is \(- 10 \left(x + 1\right)^{4}\), so it vanishes at \(x=-1\). The point is \(\left(-1,4\right)\).
The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is negative just left and negative just right, from the parity of the factor \(\left(x + 1\right)^{4}\).
This gives a stationary point of inflection. Here the second derivative also changes sign across the point.

examples.title: Use a vertical derivative vector
examples.question: The curve has parametric equations \(x=t^2+1\) and \(y=3t-2\). Use the first derivatives to find the equation of the tangent at \(t=0\).
solution: The point at \(t=0\) is \((1,-2)\). Since \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2t\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=3\), the tangent direction there is \((0,3)\).
The tangent has zero horizontal component and a non-zero vertical component. The vertical line through \((1,-2)\) is \(x=1\).

examples.title: Follow the orientation of decreasing x
examples.question: For \(x=t^{2} - 2 t + 3\) and \(y=t^{3} + 1\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
solution: Since \(x'(0)=-2\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.

The second derivative is zero at the point. Nearby, \(\frac{3 t^{2}}{2 t - 2}\) keeps the same sign on either side, because the denominator keeps the sign of \(-2\) and the numerator is a positive multiple of \(t^2\).
The curve continues the same monotonic behaviour through the horizontal tangent and changes concavity there.

extraPractice.title: Both derivatives vanish at the point
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x=t^{2} + 4\) and \(y=3 t^{3} + 2\), which statement about \(t=0\) follows from the first derivatives?
extraPractice.hint: Look at both coordinate derivatives. One vanishing component is different from both vanishing.
extraPractice.solution:
At \(t=0\), the parameter derivatives are \(0\) and \(0\).

The usual first-derivative quotient is indeterminate here. More local analysis is needed to identify a tangent.

extraPractice.title: Identify a horizontal tangent
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x=4 t + 1\) and \(y=t^{2} + 3\), which statement about \(t=0\) follows from the first derivatives?
extraPractice.hint: Look at both coordinate derivatives. One vanishing component is different from both vanishing.
extraPractice.solution:
At \(t=0\), the parameter derivatives are \(4\) and \(0\).

The motion has a nonzero horizontal derivative and zero vertical one. The tangent is horizontal.

extraPractice.title: A sixth-power local minimum
extraPractice.prompt: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=\left(x + 1\right)^{6} + 4\) at \(x=-1\).
extraPractice.hint: If the second derivative is zero, use the sign of the derivative on both sides.
extraPractice.solution:
The first derivative is \(6 \left(x + 1\right)^{5}\), so it vanishes at \(x=-1\). The point is \(\left(-1,4\right)\).

The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is negative just left and positive just right, from the parity of the factor \(\left(x + 1\right)^{5}\).

This gives a local minimum.

extraPractice.title: Use the nonzero second derivative
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x=2 t^{2} - 3 t + 1\) and \(y=2 - 2 t^{2}\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
extraPractice.hint: Check both the slope and whether local monotonicity changes. The zero second derivative alone does not classify a point.
extraPractice.solution:
Since \(x'(0)=-3\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.

The second derivative at the point is \(- \frac{4}{9}\). Its sign gives the nature of this stationary point.

The one-sided gradients have opposite signs, consistent with a local maximum.

extraPractice.title: A clear inflection despite a zero value
extraPractice.prompt: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=x^{3} + 5\) at \(x=0\).
extraPractice.hint: If the second derivative is zero, use the sign of the derivative on both sides.
extraPractice.solution:
The first derivative is \(3 x^{2}\), so it vanishes at \(x=0\). The point is \(\left(0,5\right)\).

The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is positive just left and positive just right, from the parity of the factor \(x^{2}\).

This gives a stationary point of inflection. Here the second derivative also changes sign across the point.

glossary.definition: A regular point where \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=0\).
A horizontal tangent at a point where concavity changes.
A stationary point at which the second derivative test is inconclusive.
A tangent line of the form \(x=x_0\).

revision.body:
Find where \(y'=0\) on a regular branch. A nonzero \(y''\) classifies the extremum. Otherwise compare signs of \(y'\) and analyse change of concavity.

Sign of gradient beforeSign of gradient afterConclusion
NegativePositiveLocal minimum
PositiveNegativeLocal maximum
Same signSame signNo turn. Check concavity for an inflection.
revision.checks:
• Why does \(y=x^4\) have a minimum at zero?
  • How does \(y=x^3\) behave through zero?
  • Which parameter derivatives identify a vertical tangent?
revision.examTip: State what the gradient or concavity does on each side before naming a degenerate point.

fp2_differentiation_maclaurin.description: Use derivative values to find Maclaurin coefficients, compose expansions and evaluate exact polynomial approximations.

sections.title: Why do the derivatives at zero determine the coefficients?
sections.label: Match the derivatives at zero
sections.intro: Write a trial polynomial \(a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+\cdots\). Its derivatives at zero are \(a_0,a_1,2a_2,\dots\). Matching derivatives forces the coefficients.

blocks.html: The coefficient of \(x^r\) is \(\frac{f^{(r)}(0)}{r!}\). The constant is \(f(0)\) and the coefficient of \(x\) is \(f'(0)\).
For \(x^3\) the coefficient is \(\frac{f'''(0)}6\), not \(f'''(0)\).
Keep a table with separate columns for derivative order, value at zero and coefficient.

blocks.title: Distinguish the derivative from its coefficient
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\log{\left(1 - 3 x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(2\).
blocks.hint: Include all nonzero terms from the constant through the specified degree.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=-3\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=-9\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- \frac{9 x^{2}}{2} - 3 x\).

blocks.title: Coefficient in a shifted exponential
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=2 e^{2 x}\). Give the coefficient of \(x^{3}\) in the Maclaurin expansion.
blocks.hint: Remember the factorial in each coefficient.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=2\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=4\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=8\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=16\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{8 x^{3}}{3} + 4 x^{2} + 4 x + 2\).

sections.title: What do zero derivatives and parity tell me?
sections.label: Use parity to spot missing terms
sections.intro: An even function has vanishing odd derivatives at zero, and an odd function has vanishing even derivatives there, where they exist.

blocks.html: The series for \(\cosh x\) has even powers only. The series for \(\sinh x\) or \(\tanh x\) has odd powers only. An inner shift can break the parity.
Through degree four means keep powers up to \(x^4\) even if some coefficients vanish. Four nonzero terms is a different request.
Use the stated degree or number of nonzero terms to decide where to stop.

blocks.title: An odd expansion omits even powers
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\sinh{\left(2 x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(4\).
blocks.hint: Include all nonzero terms from the constant through the specified degree.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=2\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=8\), \(f^{(4)}(0)=0\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{4 x^{3}}{3} + 2 x\).

sections.title: How do I use a known series in a composite function?
sections.label: Substitute and cap the degree
sections.intro: If a formula-booklet expansion is allowed, substitute the inner expression and discard terms only when their lowest power is beyond the target.

blocks.html: For example \(u=ax^2\) turns \(u^2\) into \(a^2x^4\). Multiplication by an outside factor can shift powers again.
A constant inside the argument means the usual local series is now centred where that argument is zero. Do not substitute a nonzero constant term blindly into a truncated series.
Write the highest required power first, then work out how many source terms can contribute.

blocks.title: Change the power by substituting
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\cos{\left(x^{2} \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(4\).
blocks.hint: Include all nonzero terms from the constant through the specified degree.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(4)}(0)=-12\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(1 - \frac{x^{4}}{2}\).

blocks.title: Keep products through the required degree
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=e^{2 x} \sin{\left(x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\).
blocks.hint: Include all nonzero terms from the constant through the specified degree.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=4\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=11\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{11 x^{3}}{6} + 2 x^{2} + x\).

sections.title: How can an equation for f′ avoid repeated quotients?
sections.label: Differentiate a simple identity
sections.intro: Seek an identity for the derivative in terms of \(f\). Differentiating it successively produces expressions you can evaluate at zero.

blocks.html: For \(f=\tanh x\), \(f'=1-f^2\), so \(f''=-2ff'\). The values \(f(0)=0\) and \(f'(0)=1\) give \(f''(0)=0\) and \(f'''(0)=-2\), hence cubic coefficient \(-\frac13\).
In \(-2ff'\), differentiating again acts on both factors and introduces \((f')^2\) as well as \(ff''\).
List enough derivative values to show the coefficient requested rather than guessing a pattern.

blocks.title: Check the sign in a tangent cubic
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\tanh{\left(3 x \right)}\). Give the coefficient of \(x^{3}\) in the Maclaurin expansion.
blocks.hint: Remember the factorial in each coefficient.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=3\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=-54\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- 9 x^{3} + 3 x\).

sections.title: What does a truncated polynomial estimate?
sections.label: Approximate near zero
sections.intro: To approximate a value, replace the function by the polynomial and state the input. Keep requested precision separate from the exact rational value of that polynomial.

blocks.html: Use \(f(x)\approx P(x)\) for a truncation. At zero the values agree. Near zero, the first omitted nonzero term often helps you judge the size of the difference.

figure.alt: Both polynomials agree with the exponential at zero. At a positive input near zero the cubic follows the exponential more closely than the linear approximation.
figure.caption: Both polynomials agree with the exponential at zero. At a positive input near zero the cubic follows the exponential more closely than the linear approximation.

blocks.html: The polynomial may approximate badly far from the centre even though its coefficients are correct.
If the question specifies a truncation, evaluate that truncation. Do not substitute a calculator value of the full function.

blocks.title: Approximate an exponential by a quadratic
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=e^{x}\). Use its Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(2\) to estimate \(f(- \frac{1}{10})\) as an exact rational number.
blocks.hint: Use the polynomial specified by the question. Do not evaluate the original function with a calculator.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=1\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{x^{2}}{2} + x + 1\).

Substituting \(x=- \frac{1}{10}\) into the polynomial gives \(\frac{181}{200}\). This is the exact value of the approximating polynomial at that input.

examples.title: Match the first three derivative values
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=\log{\left(2 x + 1 \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(2\).
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- 2 x^{2} + 2 x\).

examples.title: Recover a cubic coefficient
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=e^{- x}\). Give the coefficient of \(x^{3}\) in the Maclaurin expansion.
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- \frac{x^{3}}{6} + \frac{x^{2}}{2} - x + 1\).

examples.title: Only even powers occur in a hyperbolic cosine
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=\cosh{\left(3 x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(4\).
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{27 x^{4}}{8} + \frac{9 x^{2}}{2} + 1\).

examples.title: A substitution starts at second order
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=e^{2 x^{2}}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(4\).
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(2 x^{4} + 2 x^{2} + 1\).

examples.title: A product needs more than one source series
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=e^{x} \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\).
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + 2 x^{2} + 2 x\).

examples.title: Get the cubic term of the hyperbolic tangent
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=\tanh{\left(2 x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\).
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- \frac{8 x^{3}}{3} + 2 x\).

examples.title: Approximate the positive logarithm
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=\log{\left(x + 1 \right)}\). Use its Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\) to estimate \(f(\frac{1}{5})\) as an exact rational number.
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x\).
Substituting \(x=\frac{1}{5}\) into the polynomial gives \(\frac{137}{750}\). This is the exact value of the approximating polynomial at that input.

extraPractice.title: Give all terms through fourth degree
extraPractice.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\log{\left(x + 1 \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(4\).
extraPractice.hint: Include all nonzero terms from the constant through the specified degree.
extraPractice.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=-1\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=2\), \(f^{(4)}(0)=-6\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- \frac{x^{4}}{4} + \frac{x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + x\).

extraPractice.title: Use a rational function near zero
extraPractice.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\frac{1}{3 x + 1}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\).
extraPractice.hint: Include all nonzero terms from the constant through the specified degree.
extraPractice.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=-3\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=18\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=-162\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- 27 x^{3} + 9 x^{2} - 3 x + 1\).

extraPractice.title: Series for an inverse circular function
extraPractice.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}{\left(x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\).
extraPractice.hint: Include all nonzero terms from the constant through the specified degree.
extraPractice.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=1\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{x^{3}}{6} + x\).

extraPractice.title: Recover a fifth-order hyperbolic coefficient
extraPractice.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\sinh{\left(x \right)}\). Give the coefficient of \(x^{5}\) in the Maclaurin expansion.
extraPractice.hint: Remember the factorial in each coefficient.
extraPractice.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(4)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(5)}(0)=1\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{x^{5}}{120} + \frac{x^{3}}{6} + x\).

extraPractice.title: Estimate an even function near zero
extraPractice.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\cosh{\left(x \right)}\). Use its Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(4\) to estimate \(f(\frac{1}{3})\) as an exact rational number.
extraPractice.hint: Use the polynomial specified by the question. Do not evaluate the original function with a calculator.
extraPractice.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(4)}(0)=1\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{x^{4}}{24} + \frac{x^{2}}{2} + 1\).

Substituting \(x=\frac{1}{3}\) into the polynomial gives \(\frac{2053}{1944}\). This is the exact value of the approximating polynomial at that input.

The multiplier of a power such as \(x^3\).
Stopping a series after a specified power.
