fp2_differentiation_mixed.description: Combine implicit, parametric and inverse differentiation with local geometry and Maclaurin approximations.

sections.title: How do I choose a differentiation route?
sections.label: Read the dependency
sections.intro: A relation in \(x,y\) calls for the chain rule in \(y\). Two coordinate functions first require derivatives with respect to \(t\). In a composition, separate the outer and inner inputs.

blocks.html: Use \(F_x+F_y y'=0\) for a regular implicit point and \(y'=\frac{y_t}{x_t}\) for a regular parametric graph. Evaluate only after differentiating.
Do not replace a variable-dependent factor by its value at the target point before the next differentiation.
Label each derivative by its independent variable to avoid mixing \(x\) and \(t\).

blocks.title: Retain both derivative orders
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(1,-2\right)\) on \(- 2 X^{2} + X Y + 2 X + 2 Y^{2} + 4 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 1\) and \(Y=y + 2\), find both first and second derivatives of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).
blocks.hint: Differentiate the relationship twice while treating Y as a function of x.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(- 4 X + Y + 2+\left(X + 4 Y + 4\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(2+4y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=- \frac{1}{2}\).

Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).

At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=1\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(4\) and is nonzero.

blocks.title: Use the quotient at a negative parameter
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 3 t + 2\) and \(y=2 t^{2} + 5 t + 1\). At \(t=-1\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
blocks.hint: The derivative of the gradient with respect to t needs one further division.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 3\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 5\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t + 5}{2 t + 3}\) and hence \(1\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{2}{\left(2 t + 3\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(2\).

sections.title: Which signs and factors survive a second derivative?
sections.label: Carry the chain factors
sections.intro: Differentiate the first derivative as written, then use its local inputs to decide whether a square root sign or another chain factor is needed.

blocks.html: For \(f(u(x))\) the second derivative includes \(f''(u)(u')^2\) and \(f'(u)u''\). For a linear inner function, only the first term remains.
A correct first derivative can still give a wrong second derivative if the inner signed factor or outer branch is lost.
Check the real derivative domain before simplifying.

blocks.title: Preserve the sign of an inverse cosine
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\cos^{-1}{\left(3 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{3}{5})\) and \(f''(\frac{3}{5})\).
blocks.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
blocks.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=3 x - 1\), with derivative \(3\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(- \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - u^{2}}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=- \frac{3}{\sqrt{1 - \left(3 x - 1\right)^{2}}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{4}{5}\) to get \(-5\).

Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(- \frac{9 \left(3 x - 1\right)}{\left(1 - \left(3 x - 1\right)^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\) and so the stated value is \(- \frac{100}{3}\).

sections.title: How can I distinguish slope, curvature and line type?
sections.label: Interpret what is being requested
sections.intro: The first derivative gives the tangent gradient. The second derivative determines local concavity where finite. A normal line also needs perpendicularity and the same point.

blocks.html: At a regular horizontal tangent, use a nonzero second derivative to classify the point. When the second derivative is zero, compare the gradient around the point and check concavity if necessary.
Concavity on its own does not determine whether a point is stationary.
Give the coordinate pair and its classification separately if the question asks for both.

blocks.title: Find the perpendicular gradient for a branch
blocks.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(2,3\right)\) on \(X^{2} - 2 X Y - 3 X + 2 Y^{2} + 4 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 2\) and \(Y=y - 3\), find the gradients of the tangent and normal.
blocks.hint: Solve the first derivative equation. Then use perpendicularity.
blocks.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(2 X - 2 Y - 3+\left(- 2 X + 4 Y + 4\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(-3+4y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=\frac{3}{4}\).

Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).

At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=- \frac{5}{16}\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(4\) and is nonzero.

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so use the negative reciprocal \(- \frac{4}{3}\).

blocks.title: Read a zero second derivative in context
blocks.prompt: Identify the nature of the stationary point of \(y=\left(x + 2\right)^{4} + 4\) at \(x=-2\).
blocks.hint: If the second derivative is zero, use the sign of the derivative on both sides.
blocks.solution:
The first derivative is \(4 \left(x + 2\right)^{3}\), so it vanishes at \(x=-2\). The point is \(\left(-2,4\right)\).

The second derivative there is \(0\). The gradient is negative just left and positive just right, from the parity of the factor \(\left(x + 2\right)^{3}\).

This gives a local minimum.

sections.title: How do I use a local derivative calculation in a series?
sections.label: Build local coefficients
sections.intro: For an expression with known derivative signs or a differential identity, compute a few values at zero instead of expanding the original expression directly.

blocks.html: Use \(f^{(r)}(0)\) to form the coefficient \(\frac{f^{(r)}(0)}{r!}\). A zero derivative gives a zero term at that order.
Using a derivative as the coefficient skips the factorial, especially at orders three and four.
If a composition has been differentiated already, reuse correctly evaluated derivatives at the centre.

blocks.title: Build the first four polynomial terms
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=e^{x} \cos{\left(x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\).
blocks.hint: Include all nonzero terms from the constant through the specified degree.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=-2\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- \frac{x^{3}}{3} + x + 1\).

sections.title: What checks distinguish mathematical errors from rounding?
sections.label: Verify exactness and scope
sections.intro: Check the original domain, then check one identity against the result. If a problem uses a series, know which equality is exact for the polynomial and which is an estimate of the function.

blocks.html: Test a slope by substitution into the differentiated relation, a second derivative by its original equation, and a series by matching one derivative at zero.
A decimal near an exact radical does not establish exact equality. Keep the requested form until the end.
Make only the conclusion supported by the derivative or approximation.

blocks.title: Evaluate one exact truncation
blocks.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\log{\left(2 x + 1 \right)}\). Use its Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\) to estimate \(f(- \frac{1}{10})\) as an exact rational number.
blocks.hint: Use the polynomial specified by the question. Do not evaluate the original function with a calculator.
blocks.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=2\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=-4\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=16\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{8 x^{3}}{3} - 2 x^{2} + 2 x\).

Substituting \(x=- \frac{1}{10}\) into the polynomial gives \(- \frac{167}{750}\). This is the exact value of the approximating polynomial at that input.

examples.title: Use the product rule in an implicit relation
examples.question: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(3,-2\right)\) on \(- X^{2} + X Y + 2 X + Y^{2} + 3 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 3\) and \(Y=y + 2\), find both first and second derivatives of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).
solution: The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(- 2 X + Y + 2+\left(X + 2 Y + 3\right)y'=0\).
At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(2+3y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=- \frac{2}{3}\).
Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).
At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=\frac{22}{27}\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(3\) and is nonzero.

examples.title: Divide twice for a parametric curve
examples.question: A curve has \(x=- t^{2} + 2 t + 5\) and \(y=2 t^{2} + 3 t + 1\). At \(t=0\), calculate the first and second derivatives of y with respect to x.
solution: Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 - 2 t\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t + 3\).
Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t + 3}{2 - 2 t}\) and hence \(\frac{3}{2}\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{7}{4 \left(1 - t\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{7}{4}\).

examples.title: Differentiate an inverse after an inner shift
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\tanh^{-1}{\left(3 x - 1 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{4}{9})\) and \(f''(\frac{4}{9})\).
solution: Use the inner function \(u=3 x - 1\), with derivative \(3\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{1 - u^{2}}\).
The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{3}{1 - \left(3 x - 1\right)^{2}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{1}{3}\) to get \(\frac{27}{8}\).
Apply the chain rule once more. The second derivative is \(\frac{18 \left(3 x - 1\right)}{\left(\left(3 x - 1\right)^{2} - 1\right)^{2}}\) and so the stated value is \(\frac{243}{32}\).

examples.title: Separate tangent and normal data
examples.question: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(1,2\right)\) on \(X^{2} + 2 X Y + 3 X - Y^{2} + 5 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 1\) and \(Y=y - 2\), find the gradients of the tangent and normal.
solution: The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(2 X + 2 Y + 3+\left(2 X - 2 Y + 5\right)y'=0\).
At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(3+5y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=- \frac{3}{5}\).
Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).
At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=\frac{28}{125}\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(5\) and is nonzero.
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so use the negative reciprocal \(\frac{5}{3}\).

examples.title: Interpret a horizontal tangent after reparameterising
examples.question: For \(x=t^{2} - 2 t + 1\) and \(y=t^{3} + 3\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
solution: Since \(x'(0)=-2\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.

The second derivative is zero at the point. Nearby, \(\frac{3 t^{2}}{2 t - 2}\) keeps the same sign on either side, because the denominator keeps the sign of \(-2\) and the numerator is a positive multiple of \(t^2\).
The curve continues the same monotonic behaviour through the horizontal tangent and changes concavity there.

examples.title: Recover a cubic from a shifted inner function
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=\log{\left(1 - 2 x \right)}\). Find the complete Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\).
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(- \frac{8 x^{3}}{3} - 2 x^{2} - 2 x\).

examples.title: Keep an exact estimate separate from a function value
examples.question: Consider \(f(x)=e^{2 x}\). Use its Maclaurin polynomial through degree \(3\) to estimate \(f(\frac{1}{4})\) as an exact rational number.
solution: Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{4 x^{3}}{3} + 2 x^{2} + 2 x + 1\).
Substituting \(x=\frac{1}{4}\) into the polynomial gives \(\frac{79}{48}\). This is the exact value of the approximating polynomial at that input.

extraPractice.title: Check a principal inverse hyperbolic composition
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=\cosh^{-1}{\left(2 x - 3 \right)}\). Find the exact value of \(f'(\frac{7}{3})\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the principal derivative rule before applying the inner derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the inner function \(u=2 x - 3\), with derivative \(2\). The outer derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{u - 1} \sqrt{u + 1}}\).

The chain rule gives \(f'(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2 x - 4} \sqrt{2 x - 2}}\). Substitute \(u=\frac{5}{3}\) to get \(\frac{3}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Classify a different regular stationary point
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has \(x=t^{2} + 4 t + 3\) and \(y=2 t^{2} - 4 t + 1\). At \(t=1\), classify the point and give its second derivative.
extraPractice.hint: Verify a regular horizontal tangent before using the second-derivative test.
extraPractice.solution:
Differentiate both coordinates with respect to the parameter: \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=2 t + 4\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4 t - 4\).

Taking the quotient gives \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4 t - 4}{2 t + 4}\) and hence \(0\) at the specified parameter.

Differentiate the entire gradient with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\) again. Hence \(\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{3}{\left(t + 2\right)^{3}}\) and its value is \(\frac{1}{9}\).

The slope vanishes and the second derivative is positive. Hence the point is a local minimum.

extraPractice.title: Second derivative after a sign change
extraPractice.prompt: At the point \(P=\)\(\left(2,-1\right)\) on \(2 X^{2} + X Y - X + 2 Y^{2} + 3 Y=0\), where \(X=x - 2\) and \(Y=y + 1\), find both first and second derivatives of \(y\) with respect to \(x\).
extraPractice.hint: Differentiate the relationship twice while treating Y as a function of x.
extraPractice.solution:
The centred variables have \(\frac{\mathrm dX}{\mathrm dx}=1\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dY}{\mathrm dx}=y'\). First differentiate to obtain \(4 X + Y - 1+\left(X + 4 Y + 3\right)y'=0\).

At the point both centred variables vanish. So \(-1+3y'=0\), and \(\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_P=\frac{1}{3}\).

Differentiating that relation again uses the product rule. Before substitution the resulting equation is \(F_{XX}+2F_{XY}y'+F_{YY}(y')^2+F_Y y''=0\).

At the point, this gives \(\left.\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}\right|_P=- \frac{46}{27}\). The factor multiplying \(y''\) is \(3\) and is nonzero.

extraPractice.title: Distinguish derivative value and coefficient
extraPractice.prompt: Consider \(f(x)=\tanh{\left(x \right)}\). Give the coefficient of \(x^{5}\) in the Maclaurin expansion.
extraPractice.hint: Remember the factorial in each coefficient.
extraPractice.solution:
Find the derivatives at zero. Here \(f^{(0)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(1)}(0)=1\), \(f^{(2)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(3)}(0)=-2\), \(f^{(4)}(0)=0\), \(f^{(5)}(0)=16\).

Divide each derivative of order \(r\) by \(r!\) and multiply by \(x^r\). The resulting polynomial is \(\frac{2 x^{5}}{15} - \frac{x^{3}}{3} + x\).

extraPractice.title: Check a maximum with negative parameter speed
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x=t^{2} - 3 t + 2\) and \(y=4 - 2 t^{2}\), classify the point at \(t=0\).
extraPractice.hint: Check both the slope and whether local monotonicity changes. The zero second derivative alone does not classify a point.
extraPractice.solution:
Since \(x'(0)=-3\) is nonzero and \(y'(0)=0\), this is a regular stationary point.

The second derivative at the point is \(- \frac{4}{9}\). Its sign gives the nature of this stationary point.

The one-sided gradients have opposite signs, consistent with a local maximum.

glossary.definition: The way one coordinate or function varies with its input.
A derivative obtained from a relation in \(x\) and \(y\) without isolating \(y\).
The derivative of the inner function introduced when differentiating a composition.
The point where the derivatives used for the series are evaluated.

revision.body: Choose the derivative method from the relation. Check \(F_y\) or \(x_t\) before division. In a series, compute \(f^{(r)}(0)\) before dividing by \(r!\).
revision.checks:
• Which part of your setup ensures the local derivative is defined?
  • How can a derivative sign verify a graph?
  • Does your stated value belong to the original function or its truncation?
revision.examTip: Carry exact values throughout the derivative steps, then give the requested form and precision.
